## The idea

Play four bars that stop on G, pause, then replay their opening and end on C.
The first half sets a boundary without closing the larger shape. The second half
answers it. Much of the effect can live in the last two notes.

An *antecedent* is a phrase that behaves like a question, often ending with a
half cadence. A *consequent* answers it with stronger closure, often an authentic
cadence. Together they form a *period*. The two phrases need enough shared
material to sound related and enough difference at the boundary to sound
directed.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |events|
  events.each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

opening = [[:c4, 1], [:e4, 1], [:g4, 1], [:e4, 1],
           [:f4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]]

question_tail = [[:d4, 1], [:f4, 1], [:g4, 2]]
answer_tail = [[:d4, 1], [:b3, 1], [:c4, 2]]

antecedent = opening + question_tail
consequent = opening + answer_tail

play_phrase antecedent
sleep 1
play_phrase consequent
sleep 2

# A broken pair: the question closes before the answer arrives.
play_phrase opening + answer_tail
sleep 1
play_phrase consequent
```

The first pair shares its opening and diverges at the cadence. G leaves the
antecedent open; C closes the consequent. In the second pair, the first phrase
already arrives on C, so the repeated closure has less work to do.

## Change one thing

1. Change only the question's final G to C. The two phrases now compete to sound
   final, weakening the eight-bar arc.
2. Transpose the consequent opening up two semitones while keeping its answer
   tail. The relation becomes less literal and the return to C more abrupt.
3. Remove the one-beat pause. Silence helps the phrase boundary register; without
   it, rhythm and cadence must carry the division alone.

## Why it works

A period combines repetition and contrast. Shared opening data establishes that
the two phrases belong to one object. Different suffixes alter their cadential
function. In programming terms, each phrase is a common prefix plus a parameterised
tail.

The question ends on degree 5, the dominant. Lesson 29 treated a final V as a
half cadence because it predicts continuation. The answer moves through the
leading tone B to tonic C, giving the strongest local arrival available in the
key. Melody and harmony can reinforce the same punctuation even when this small
example states the chords only by implication.

Four plus four bars is a common scale for a period, not a parser rule. A phrase
is perceived through grouping, repetition, breath, duration, and cadence. The
code exposes two of those cues: shared data and contrasting endings. A richer
arrangement can add dynamics and accompaniment without changing the structure.

The repeated opening also sets an expectation about timing. When the consequent
begins with the same seven events, you can predict where its tail will diverge.
Shorten the second opening and the answer may arrive too early to feel balanced.
Lengthen it and the memory of the antecedent weakens. Symmetry is therefore one
available design, not a requirement imposed by the data type.

An answer can vary more than its cadence. It may begin higher, compress the
rhythm, or reverse one interval while preserving the opening gesture. Make one
change at a time during drafting. If pitch, rhythm, register, and harmony all
change together, the listener has little evidence that the second phrase answers
the first rather than starting a new section.

## Take it further

Create a period in A minor. Reuse one two-bar opening in both phrases. End the
antecedent on E and the consequent on A, using G-sharp in the answer to create
the harmonic-minor leading tone. Keep each phrase at exactly eight beats and
print a bar-total assertion before playing.
